dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematically read the reference source: Gemfile, config.ru, full app.rb in chunks, all models, lib/*, db.rb, migrations, seeds, jobs/runner.rb, all liquid views, and specs — enumerating routes/models/templates before writing Rust.

Started the reference via rackup and ran differential curls across many subsystems (tags, feeds, login/register HTML, admin, posts, comments, 404/405, audit log), empirically catching edge cases (RSS timezone/indent, markdown rel attrs, Sinatra 404-vs-405, .to_i path semantics) and revisiting the reference as each mismatch surfaced.

Probed cross-runtime job-queue concerns: read jobs/runner.rb and job model, reasoned about BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics, and diagnosed the Sequel schema_info migration-tracking conflict on the shared DB.

Repeatedly declared 'I have enough understanding' and pivoted to building under perceived time pressure; RJ_* env vars, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, CSP contents, and pagination link format were taken from code-reading and never empirically confirmed against the live reference, and no durable notes/tables model was built.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond anchor 5's 'handful of endpoints': it read all major reference files, enumerated subsystems, then ran sustained live differential probing that caught numerous edge cases and repeatedly returned to the reference as mismatches emerged — a self-correcting, empirical orientation approaching anchor 8. But it stops short of 8/10 because coverage was incomplete (no explicit RJ_* enumeration; rate-limit, ETag, CSP, and pagination contracts never empirically verified) and it kept no durable behavioral reference model, working reactively rather than methodically mapping every subsystem. This places it at a 7, between anchors 5 and 8.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: After reading the reference, agent states 'This is a massive project... Let me prioritize - I'll need to be strategic' and 'focus on parity for structurally tested behaviors' — genuine intent to decompose but expressed as a vague mental list with no written milestone breakdown or per-piece completion criteria.

Wrote all subsystems as modules in a natural dependency order (db.rs/schema.sql → models → md → templates → jobs → handlers chunked by feature: accounts, posts, comments, tags, search, media, feeds, admin). Shows an implicit sensible decomposition, but built everything in a single push with no per-subsystem done-check before moving on.
Only after all modules were written did the agent build once and start reactively probing endpoints — verification was not planned as a milestone exit test but happened as a bunched post-build phase.

The foundational, high-risk shared-DB / cross-runtime schema_info migration concern was discovered reactively at the very end after the reference failed to migrate — a dependency that a dependency-aware milestone plan would have sequenced early, indicating sequencing was emergent rather than risk-tiered.
Late-stage subsystem work (markdown rel attrs, 404/405 routing, path-param parsing) handled as a reactive punch-list of parity diffs, not as pre-defined milestones with exit tests.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent had a real, sensibly-ordered module decomposition (schema/db before feeds/handlers) which lifts it above a purely monolithic effort, but there was never an explicit written milestone plan with per-subsystem completion criteria; strategic statements stayed vague ('be strategic', 'prioritize'). Construction was a one-shot 'write everything then build once' push with verification bunched reactively at the end, and the riskiest shared-state interface (cross-runtime schema/migration) was discovered late rather than sequenced first. This matches the level-3 anchor ('vague mental list, no explicit completion criteria') with a partial lean toward level-5's sensible ordering and rough post-hoc done-signals, placing it at a 4.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Stood up the real Ruby reference (rackup:8001) alongside the Rust server (:8000) and began side-by-side curl comparisons of endpoints — genuine differential setup against the reference, not just 'it compiles'.
Compared RSS/Atom feeds between both servers and caught concrete mismatches (timezone -0000 vs +0000, </channel> indentation), then fixed them — differential diffing catching body mismatches.
Compared login HTML using diff with `tr -s ' \t\n' ' '` whitespace collapse — a manual normalization mirroring one grader rule, but one-off, not a reusable harness.
Ad-hoc comparisons of markdown output (missing rel attr), audit-log entries, and status codes; all fresh manual curls repeated after each rebuild rather than an automated regression harness.

Only reasoned about the cross-runtime shared-DB/job-queue semantics (schema co-existence, BEGIN IMMEDIATE) — did not build an actual test exercising the shared job queue against the reference, so the '8' anchor's queue interop is absent.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent ran the real reference beside its own service and manually diffed responses across many subsystems (JSON APIs, feeds, HTML, markdown, audit log, status codes), catching numerous real mismatches — clearly beyond the level-3 'few curls, no reuse.' However every check was an ad-hoc, one-shot curl/diff with only minimal manual normalization (whitespace collapse), no reusable harness reflecting the grader's normalization (dynamic-key elision, header-as-set, UUID/timestamp normalization), and no exercise of the cross-runtime job queue, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, or concurrency. That matches anchor 5 rather than 8.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Verification is ad-hoc curl-vs-reference on individual endpoints (tags, feeds, posts) with no written checklist of which subsystems pass/fail; coverage exists only as loose recollection.

Notices a real posts_count divergence, calls it 'concerning', investigates briefly, then explicitly moves on to 'other tests' without tracking it as an unresolved failing area — no ledger of open gaps.

After edits to shared handlers.rs (content-type, RSS spacing, markdown rel, 404/405, path parsing) the agent rebuilds and re-tests only the touched endpoint, never re-running previously-passing areas — no regression guard on shared code.

Declares task complete based on a handful of manual matches plus binary-size/start.sh presence, with no coverage accounting of attempted-vs-remaining subsystems (media, FTS search, job queue, pagination largely unverified).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained only a vague mental picture of parity coverage, sweeping across several subsystems via manual curl comparisons but never keeping a running checklist, distinguishing passing/failing/not-attempted, or re-testing previously-passing areas after touching shared code (matching anchor [3]). It exceeds [0] because it did probe multiple subsystems and noticed individual mismatches, but it never reaches [5]'s maintained, updated checklist, and there is no harness-backed ledger or explicit thrash detection, so the [8]/[10] behaviors are absent.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Diagnoses that the Ruby reference (Sequel) fails to migrate over a Rust-created schema, roots it in Sequel's schema_info version tracking, and adds a schema_info(version=14) table — a design-level, cross-runtime root-cause correction re-derived from reference behavior.

Recognizes framework-limitation classes: axum returns 405 vs Sinatra 404, and Path<i64> yields 400 vs reference 404/401. Fixes at router level (method_not_allowed_fallback) and switches to String+manual parse — treats recurring mismatch as a design signal, not a one-off patch.
Applies the String-path parsing fix across the whole follow/unfollow/followers/following handler class, generalizing a correction rather than fixing a single instance.

Returns to reference to correct RSS timezone/indent and adds markdown rel-attribute post-processing — genuine reference-driven correction but symptom-level (patches pulldown_cmark output instead of reconsidering the approach).
Flags posts_count divergence as 'concerning' and investigates, but effectively moves on without a design revision — a falsified assumption left partly unresolved, keeping it below the top anchor.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently returns to the reference to recover true behavior and correct implementation (level 5), and several times escalates beyond local patches to design-level fixes that address a whole class of failures — router-level method/404 handling, cross-runtime schema_info tracking, and String-path parsing applied across handlers (edging toward 8). However, it never makes a decisive library/model swap when a component (markdown) diverges, does not systematically re-verify entire affected subsystems, and leaves at least one flagged divergence (posts_count) unresolved. This places it between the level-5 and level-8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Verified release binary size (6.3MB) against the 40MB cap twice, including as a final check — more than a one-time glance.

Actively guarded shared-DB interop: discovered Sequel migrator conflict when reference starts against a Rust-created schema, added schema_info version tracking, and re-tested both runtimes co-existing on the same /app/data/rj.db.
Explicitly reasoned about BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics for the cross-runtime job queue, treating it as a matched contract.
Process-tree/no-Ruby check is weak: the ps aux grep was to see if the reference was up, and the planned 'check no Ruby processes' final audit was never actually executed (only ls of start.sh).
Latency parity constraint essentially unguarded — noted Mutex may serialize requests but dismissed it as 'acceptable' without ever measuring the /_health latency ratio.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went beyond the level-5 anchor (verify obvious constraints once): it checked binary size multiple times and, most notably, treated the shared-DB BEGIN IMMEDIATE/migration interop as a real matched contract, actively debugging and re-testing cross-runtime co-existence (steps 94-99). However it falls short of level 8: the /_health latency ratio was never measured, the no-Ruby process-tree audit was planned but not actually executed, and Cargo.toml was never audited for banned bridge crates. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors — genuine, targeted guarding of some constraints but not all — landing at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
